title: Cache Organization and Mapping
subtitle: Tags, indexes, offsets and the three ways to place a block.

references.title: Large and Fast: Exploiting Memory Hierarchy
references.topics: The basics of caches: direct-mapped caches, tags and valid bits, handling hits and misses; associative caches: set-associative and fully associative placement

objectives: Define block, line, tag, index, offset and valid bit
Split an address into tag, index and offset
Trace hits and misses in direct-mapped, set-associative and fully associative caches
Explain how associativity removes conflict misses
Calculate tag bits and total cache storage

steps.question: A cache holds a few thousand blocks out of billions of addresses. How can the hardware check in a single cycle whether the one you want is there?
clues: Each address maps to **one place** (or a small set of places).
A **tag** says which block currently lives there.
The address itself is cut into **tag, index and offset**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: The vocabulary

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The unit copied between memory and cache (several neighbouring bytes)
One place in the cache that can hold one block
1 if the line holds real data, 0 if empty (e.g. at start-up)
The high bits of the block address, stored with the line to say which block it is
The address bits that select the line (or set)
The low address bits that select the byte inside the block

steps.why: Every cache lookup uses exactly these pieces.
steps.real: Whenever a cache is described as "32 KB, 8-way, 64-byte lines" it is giving the numbers that fix these fields.

explainAgain.beginner: A hotel: the index is the floor, the tag is the guest's name on the register, and the offset is the bed in the room.

steps.title: Cutting up an address

nodes.label: Offset
nodes.note: log2(block size) bits: byte inside the block.

nodes.label: Index
nodes.note: log2(number of sets) bits: which line or set.

nodes.label: Tag
nodes.note: Compared with the tag stored in the line.

terms.t: offset bits = log2(block size in bytes)
tag bits = address bits − index bits − offset bits

steps.why: The split is fixed by the cache design, so the hardware can pick out each field with wires, no calculation.
steps.real: This is why cache sizes and block sizes are always powers of two.

mistake.wrong: The index comes from the highest address bits.
mistake.right: The tag takes the highest bits; the index sits just above the offset.

steps.title: Try it: split an address

blocks.title: Tag, index and offset

stages.label: Index
stages.text: The next {ib} bits: **{mod(floor(addr / pow(2, ob)), pow(2, ib))}**

stages.label: Tag
stages.text: The remaining {16 - ob - ib} bits: **{floor(addr / pow(2, ob + ib))}**

blocks.result: {addr|hex4}: tag {floor(addr / pow(2, ob + ib))}, index {mod(floor(addr / pow(2, ob)), pow(2, ib))}, offset {mod(addr, pow(2, ob))}
blocks.note: The default is 0x1234 with 16-byte blocks and 8 lines (direct-mapped): tag 36, index 3, offset 4.

steps.why: Change the number of offset or index bits and watch which field grows.

steps.question: A direct-mapped cache has 8 lines and 16-byte blocks. Which index does address 0x1234 use?

reveal.text: Offset = 0x1234 mod 16 = 4. Block number = 0x1234 ÷ 16 = 291. Index = 291 mod 8 = **3**. Tag = 291 ÷ 8 = 36.

steps.result: Index = block number mod number of sets.

steps.question: A cache has 16-byte blocks. How many offset bits are there?
feedback: 16 is the block size, not the number of bits.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each field with its job.

pairs.b: Selects the byte inside the block
Says whether the line holds real data

steps.title: One block, one line

items: Each memory block can go to **exactly one line**: index = block number mod number of lines
Lookup: use the index to read one line; compare its tag with the address tag; check the valid bit
Match and valid: **hit**. Otherwise **miss**: fetch the block and replace what was there
Simple, fast and cheap: only **one** tag comparison

head: Step
Action
rows: Read the line at the index
Valid and tags equal? Hit: use the offset to pick the data
Otherwise miss: bring the block from the next level and store tag + data

steps.why: Direct mapping gives the fastest lookup, at the cost of conflicts between blocks that share a line.
steps.real: Small, fast caches and TLBs sometimes use direct mapping.

mistake.wrong: A cache line can hold any block.
mistake.right: In a direct-mapped cache each block has exactly one possible line.

steps.title: A trace

blocks.text: Cache: **4 lines**, **4-byte blocks**, 8-bit addresses. Access addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 16, 0.

steps.why: Blocks 0 and 4 both map to line 0, so they keep evicting each other. That is a **conflict miss**.
steps.real: Strided access patterns hit this problem often.

steps.title: Try it: direct-mapped

blocks.title: Direct-mapped cache
blocks.hint: Step through **Trace above**; then run **Conflicts** (addresses 0 and 16 share line 0).

steps.why: The trace gives 1 hit and 6 misses. Conflicts: 0 hits in 6 accesses even though the cache is almost empty.

steps.question: Addresses 0 and 16 are read alternately, six accesses, in this direct-mapped cache (4 lines, 4-byte blocks). How many hits?

reveal.text: Both addresses map to line 0 (blocks 0 and 4, index 0). Each access evicts the other's block: **0 hits**, 6 misses, 4 of them conflict misses.

steps.result: Three of the four lines stay empty. The problem is placement, not capacity.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about direct-mapped caches is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. Each block can be placed in exactly one line.
2. The index is block number mod number of lines.
3. Two blocks with the same index can both stay in the cache.
4. Only one tag comparison is needed per lookup.
steps.explain: Two blocks with the same index compete for one line, so only one can be present.
steps.fix: Blocks that share an index evict each other.

steps.statement: A valid bit of 0 means the line holds no usable data.
steps.why: This is how an empty cache is recognised after start-up.

steps.title: More freedom in placement

head: Organisation
Where a block may go
Comparisons per lookup
rows: Any of the n lines in one set (set = block mod number of sets)

terms.note: index selects a set, not a line
tag = all bits above the offset

steps.why: More choices for each block means fewer evictions between blocks that happen to share an index.
steps.real: L1 caches are typically 4- or 8-way; L2 and L3 use more ways. Fully associative caches are used only when small (like a TLB).

explainAgain.beginner: Hotel with floors: direct mapped = one room per guest; 2-way = two rooms to pick from on your floor; fully associative = any room in the hotel.

steps.title: Replacement: LRU

items: When a set is full a block must be **evicted**
**LRU** (least recently used) evicts the block unused for the longest time
LRU uses temporal locality: a block used recently is likely to be used again
Real caches approximate LRU to keep the hardware cheap

steps.why: Associativity needs a replacement policy; direct mapped has none, because each block has only one place.
steps.real: Random replacement is also used and performs nearly as well in large caches.

steps.title: Try it: associativity

blocks.title: Same 4 lines, different associativity
blocks.hint: Switch **associativity** between 1-way, 2-way and fully associative (4 lines in total).

steps.why: Conflicts: direct mapped 0 hits of 6; 2-way and fully associative 4 hits of 6. Cycle of three blocks: direct 0, 2-way 0, fully associative 3 hits.

steps.question: Three blocks that map to the same set are read in a cycle: 0, 16, 32, 0, 16, 32. A 2-way LRU cache with 4 lines: how many hits?

reveal.text: The set holds only 2 blocks but the cycle needs 3. With LRU the block about to be used is always the one just evicted: **0 hits**. A fully associative 4-line cache holds all three and gets 3 hits.

steps.result: Associativity helps up to a point; a cycle bigger than the set still thrashes.

questions.a: The line (direct mapped) or the set (set associative).

questions.q: Why do conflict misses occur in a direct-mapped cache?
questions.a: Several blocks share one line and evict each other.
A block may go in several lines of a set, so fewer evictions.

steps.title: Comparing the three
steps.why: Associativity removes conflict misses but costs more comparators, more power and a slower lookup.
steps.real: Doubling associativity gives diminishing returns beyond about 4 to 8 ways.

mistake.right: It reduces conflicts but makes the lookup slower and larger.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put a set-associative lookup in order.
items: Split the address into tag, index and offset
Use the index to select a set
Compare the tag with every valid line in the set
Hit: use the offset to select the data. Miss: fetch the block and replace the LRU line
steps.why: The index narrows the search before any comparison.

steps.question: A cache has 16 lines and is 4-way set associative. How many sets does it have?
feedback: Sets cannot exceed the number of lines.

steps.title: How many bits does a cache really need?

items: Each line stores **data**, a **tag** and a **valid bit**
Bits per line = 1 + tag bits + 8 × block bytes
Total bits = number of lines × bits per line
The tag and valid bits are **overhead**: the cache holds more bits than its data capacity

steps.why: The data capacity (for example 1 KiB) is only part of the real hardware cost.
steps.real: Larger blocks mean fewer tags per byte of data, so less overhead.

deeper.text: Real caches also keep LRU bits and, for write-back, a dirty bit (Class 19).

steps.title: Calculate: bits and storage

blocks.title: Cache bit counts
blocks.equation: Everything follows from the sizes (all powers of two)

results.label: Total bits
results.formula: pow(2, sz - bl) * (1 + (ab - (sz - bl - al) - bl) + 8 * pow(2, bl))

steps.why: With the defaults (32-bit addresses, 1 KiB direct mapped, 16-byte blocks): 64 lines, 6 index bits, 4 offset bits, 22 tag bits, 151 bits per line, 9,664 bits in total. Raise the associativity and the tag grows by one bit per doubling.

steps.question: 1 KiB direct-mapped cache, 16-byte blocks, 32-bit addresses. How many tag bits?

reveal.text: Lines = 1024 ÷ 16 = 64, so index = 6 bits; offset = 4 bits; tag = 32 − 6 − 4 = **22 bits**.

steps.result: Doubling the associativity moves one bit from the index to the tag.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why does a cache with 64-byte blocks need fewer tag bits per byte of data than one with 4-byte blocks of the same size?
steps.answer: There are 16 times fewer lines with 64-byte blocks, so only a sixteenth as many tags and valid bits for the same data capacity. Larger blocks also exploit spatial locality, but they raise the miss penalty (Class 19).

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: You have 4 KiB of cache. Would you choose direct mapped, 4-way or fully associative, and why?
ideas: Direct mapped: simplest and fastest, but conflict misses.
4-way: removes most conflict misses with a modest cost.
Fully associative: fewest conflicts but a slow, power-hungry comparison of every tag.
Most real L1 caches choose a middle value (4 to 8 ways).

steps.question: Name the three parts an address is split into for a cache lookup, from the low bits upward.
steps.solution: Offset (byte in the block), then index (which line or set), then the tag.

steps.question: 16-bit addresses, direct-mapped cache with 8 lines of 16 bytes. Split address 0x1234 into tag, index and offset.
steps.solution: Offset = 0x1234 mod 16 = 4. Block = 291. Index = 291 mod 8 = 3. Tag = 291 ÷ 8 = 36. Bits: 9 + 3 + 4 = 16.
steps.hint: Offset bits = log2(16) = 4; index bits = log2(8) = 3.
steps.mistake: Taking the index from the top bits.

steps.question: 32-bit addresses, 64 lines, 16-byte blocks, direct mapped. How many tag, index and offset bits?
For the same cache, how many bits of storage are needed in total (valid bit, tag, data)?
steps.solution: Per line: 1 + 22 + 128 = 151. Total 64 × 151 = 9,664 bits (1,024 bytes = 8,192 data bits plus 1,472 bits of overhead).
steps.hint: Data per line is 8 × block bytes.

steps.question: Cache: 4 lines, 4-byte blocks, direct mapped, 8-bit addresses. Accesses 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 16, 0. Give hit or miss for each and the number of hits.
steps.answer: M M M M H M M; 1 hit. The last miss is a conflict miss.
steps.solution: Blocks 0 to 3 fill lines 0 to 3. Address 0 hits. Address 16 (block 4) maps to line 0 and evicts block 0, so the final 0 misses.

steps.question: Same accesses and cache size, but 2-way set associative with LRU. How many hits? Which accesses hit?
steps.answer: 2 hits: the second access of address 0 and the last access of address 0.
steps.solution: Two sets; blocks 0 and 2 go in set 0, blocks 1 and 3 in set 1. Address 16 (block 4) also maps to set 0: it evicts block 2 (least recently used), not block 0, so the final 0 still hits.
steps.title: Exam practice: trace

steps.question: Compare direct-mapped, 2-way and fully associative (4 lines in total) on 0, 16, 32, 0, 16, 32. Give the hits for each and explain the 2-way result.
steps.solution: Blocks 0, 4 and 8 map to the same set (set 0 for 2 sets). The cycle of three does not fit in 2 ways, so LRU always evicts the block needed next. The fully associative cache holds all three after the first round.
steps.title: Exam practice: conflicts

steps.question: A 4 KiB, 2-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses. Give lines, sets, offset, index, tag bits and the total storage in bits.
steps.answer: 128 lines, 64 sets; offset 5, index 6, tag 21; total 35,584 bits.
steps.mistake: Using the number of lines instead of the number of sets for the index.
steps.title: Exam practice: storage

steps.question: A fully associative cache has 8 lines of 4 bytes and 16-bit addresses. Give the tag bits and the total storage in bits.
steps.solution: Offset 2 bits; there is one set so index = 0 bits; tag = 16 − 2 = 14. Per line 1 + 14 + 32 = 47; 8 × 47 = 376.
steps.title: Exam practice: fully associative

steps.question: 16-bit addresses, direct-mapped, 8 lines of 16 bytes. Accesses: 0x1234, 0x1238, 0x2234, 0x1234. Give hit or miss and the miss type for each.
steps.solution: 0x1234 and 0x1238 are in the same block (index 3, tag 36). 0x2234 has index 3 but tag 68, so it replaces the first block. The final 0x1234 misses because its block was evicted.
steps.mistake: Treating 0x1238 as a miss: it is in the same 16-byte block.
steps.title: Exam practice: hit or miss
What you should remember
remember: A block is the unit copied; a line holds one block with a valid bit and a tag.
Address = tag | index | offset. offset = log2(block bytes); index = log2(sets); tag = the rest.
Direct mapped: index = block mod lines; one comparison; conflict misses.
n-way set associative: sets = lines ÷ n; LRU replacement; fewer conflicts; n comparisons.
Fully associative: one set, any line, tag = all bits above the offset.
Total bits = lines × (1 + tag + 8 × block bytes).

mistakes.wrong: The index comes from the high bits.
mistakes.right: The tag takes the high bits; the index is just above the offset.
A cycle larger than the set still thrashes, and lookups get slower.

mistakes.wrong: Cache size equals the bits stored.
mistakes.right: Tags and valid bits add overhead.

mistakes.wrong: All bytes of a block are separate misses.
mistakes.right: A miss brings the whole block.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: An address is cut into tag, index and offset. In a direct-mapped cache each block has one possible line, giving a fast lookup but conflict misses. Set-associative and fully associative caches let a block go in several places, trading extra comparators for fewer conflicts. The tag, valid bit and data bits together set the real storage cost.
